The '''South Florida Detention Facility''', nicknamed '''''Alligator Alcatraz''''',<ref name="Borresen 08222025"/><ref>{{cite news |last1=Bridges |first1=C.A. |title=Judge stops work at Florida's 'Alligator Alcatraz.' What are they building there? |url=https://www.palmbeachpost.com/story/news/politics/2025/08/08/alligator-alcatraz-florida-constriction-halted-district-judge/85572691007/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250808230956/https://www.palmbeachpost.com/story/news/politics/2025/08/08/alligator-alcatraz-florida-constriction-halted-district-judge/85572691007/ |url-status=dead |archive-date=August 8, 2025|access-date=8 September 2025|newspaper=[[The Palm Beach Post]]|date=8 August 2025}}</ref> was an [[Immigration detention in the United States|immigration detention]] facility located on historical [[Native American]] lands at [[Dade-Collier Training and Transition Airport]] inside [[Big Cypress National Preserve]] in [[Ochopee, Florida]], United States.<ref>{{Cite news|last=|date=2026-05-12|title=Detainees will move out of 'Alligator Alcatraz,' facility to shut down by June, source says |url=https://www.nbcmiami.com/news/local/alligator-alcatraz-immigation-detention-center-closure/3808365/|access-date=2026-06-22|publisher=[[NBC 6 South Florida]]|language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |date=2026-05-14 |title=Florida Everglades "Alligator Alcatraz" Staying Put Despite Price Tag, Fire Risks |url=https://www.tampafp.com/florida-everglades-alligator-alcatraz-staying-put-despite-price-tag-fire-risks/|access-date=2026-06-22|newspaper=Tampa Free Press|language=en-US}}</ref> The [[Florida Division of Emergency Management]] detained non-citizens under [[Immigration and Customs Enforcement]] authority from July 2025 to June 2026<ref>{{cite news|last=Charalambous|first=Peter |last2=Pecorin |first2=Allison  |date=August 20, 2025 |title=Democratic lawmakers demand information about 'Alligator Alcatraz': The Trump administration is using state-run facilities to detain noncitizens. |url=https://abcnews.com/US/democratic-lawmakers-demand-information-alligator-alcatraz/story?id=124780232|publisher=[[ABC News (United States)|ABC News]]}}</ref><ref name="auto12">Payne, Kate. ''FloridaTrib''.</ref> at an estimated cost of at least US$1.4 billion in unnegotiated contracts.<ref name="Caputo 09042026">{{cite news|last=Caputo|first=Liz|last2=Heddles |first2=Claire |date=September 4, 2026 |title=FL immigration contracts quietly surged to $1.4B in disaster dollars|url=https://www.miamiherald.com/news/politics-government/state-politics/article317119382.html|newspaper=[[Miami Herald]]}}</ref> Multiple media outlets have reported that several no-bid private businesses also made campaign donations to DeSantis’ PACs and Attorney General James Uthmeier.<ref>{{cite news |date=October 7, 2025 |title=Did ‘dirty money’ help win ‘Alligator Alcatraz’ contracts?|url=https://votewater.org/did-dirty-money-help-win-alligator-alcatraz-contracts/ |work=VoteWater}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|date=July 7, 2026|title=The Staggering Cost of James Uthmeier |first=Brad|last=Norman|url=https://www.thebradentontimes.com/stories/the-staggering-cost-of-james-uthmeier,204150|work=The Bradenton Times}}</ref>

== Location ==
Located in [[the Everglades]], the [[Big Cypress]] area was historically occupied by various cultures of [[Native Americans]]; the descendants include the federally recognized [[Miccosukee Tribe of Indians of Florida]] and the [[Seminole Tribe of Florida]]. The construction of a new Miami Jetport began on site in 1968 as [[Dade-Collier Training and Transition Airport|Everglades Jetport.]] In 1969, [[Marjory Stoneman Douglas]], author of ''[[The Everglades: River of Grass]]'', founded [[Friends of the Everglades]]. Construction was halted in 1970 due to efforts of Native Americans including [[Buffalo Tiger]], hunters, [[Environmental Impact of the Big Cypress Swamp Jetport|environmental concerns related to the Big Cypress Swamp]] and the cancellation of the [[Boeing 2707|2707 Boeing]] program. By that point, one {{convert|10,500|ft|m|adj=mid}} runway was built, the facility occupying 39 square miles (100&nbsp;km<sup>2</sup>).<ref name="freeman">{{cite web|last1=Freeman|first1=Paul|title=Everglades Jetport / Dade Collier Training & Transition Airport (TNT), Everglades, FL|url=https://www.airieldsfreeman.com/FL/Airfields_FL_Miami_N.htm#dade|access-date=5 February 2016}}</ref>

Following continued efforts to federally protect the area, Big Cypress National Preserve became one of the first [[National preserves]] in the [[List of areas in the National Park System of the United States|United States National Park System]] on October 11, 1974.<ref name=nps>{{cite web|url=https://www.nps.gov/bicy/index.htm|title=Big Cypress|publisher=[[National Park Service]]|access-date=2016-02-20}}</ref> According to [[Miami-Dade County Mayor]] [[Daniella Levine Cava]], since 2019, the federal and state governments had previously invested well over $10 billion in Everglades restoration and protection.<ref name="AP-20250806"/> The Big Cypress National Preserve provides the [[Miccosukee]], [[Seminole]] and Traditional people with permanent rights to occupy and use the land in traditional ways. In addition, they have first rights to develop income-producing businesses related to the resources and use of the preserve, such as guided tours.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.nps.gov/history/history/online_books/bicy/miccosukee_seminole_indians.pdf|publisher=[[National Park Service]]|author=Goss, James A.|title=Usual and Customary Use by the Miccosukee and Seminole Indians in Big Cypress National Preserve, Florida|date=1995|page=4-5|archive-date=January 14, 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120114065553/http://www.nps.gov/history/history/online_books/bicy/miccosukee_seminole_indians.pdf}}</ref>

Big Cypress National Preserve was designated a [[DarkSky International]] park in 2016; the nation's first preserve to achieve "dark sky" status.<ref>{{cite web|author=Chesnes, Max|date=July 18, 2025|url=https://www.tampabay.com/news/environment/2025/07/09/alligator-alcatraz-light-pollution-florida-everglades-big-cypress/|title=Darkness is crucial to Everglades habitat. Could Alligator Alcatraz threaten it? Artificial light in a world-renowned 'dark sky' preserve is just one of the environmental and human health concerns surrounding the facility.|newspaper=[[Tampa Bay Times]]|access-date=September 27, 2025}}</ref>

[https://www.americanimmigrationcouncil.org/press-release/congress-approves-unprecedented-funding-mass-detention-deportation-2025/ "Senate Approves Unprecedented Spending for Mass Deportation, Ignoring What's Broken in our Immigration System"]. Retrieved August 18, 2025.</ref><ref name="Brownstein">{{Cite news |last=Brownstein |first=Ronald |date=February 8, 2024|title=Trump's 'Knock on the Door' |url=https://www.theatlantic.com/politics/archive/2024/02/trumps-immigration-plan-is-even-more-aggressive-now/677385/|url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240210204500/https://www.theatlantic.com/politics/archive/2024/02/trumps-immigration-plan-is-even-more-aggressive-now/677385/|archive-date=February 10, 2024|access-date=February 11, 2024|magazine=[[The Atlantic]]|language=en-US}}</ref>

===Opening===
On June 19, 2025, the "Alligator Alcatraz" was announced, which sources later officially named the "South Florida Detention Facility".<ref name="Borresen 08222025">{{Cite news |last1=Borresen |first1=Jennifer|last2=Loehrke |first2=Janet|last3=Beard|first3=Stephen J.|last4=Sullivan|first4=Shawn J. |last5=Petras |first5=George |date=August 22, 2025 |title=Will Alligator Alcatraz close? Here's a look inside the controversial detention center|work=[[USA Today]]|url=https://www.usatoday.com/story/graphics/2025/08/22/alligator-alcatraz-detention-center-maps-details/85258104007/|url-access=subscription |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250826070239/https://www.usatoday.com/story/graphics/2025/08/22/alligator-alcatraz-detention-center-maps-details/85258104007/ |archive-date=2025-08-26 |access-date=2025-12-09 }}{{cbignore}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|last=Bridges|first=C.A.|date=August 29, 2025|title=Why is 'Alligator Alcatraz' closing? What Florida immigrant detention center cos|newspaper=[[The Palm Beach Post]]|url=https://www.palmbeachpost.com/story/news/2025/08/29/alligator-alcatraz-closure-florida/85883999007/|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250829160656/https://www.palmbeachpost.com/story/news/2025/08/29/alligator-alcatraz-closure-florida/85883999007/|url-status=dead|archive-date=August 29, 2025|access-date=August 30, 2025}}</ref> According to the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement website, the official name is the "Florida Soft Sided Facility South".<ref>U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement. (not dated) [https://www.ice.gov/detain/detention-facilities/florida-soft-sided-facility-south Florida Soft Sided Facility South]</ref> Signs outside the camp indicated "Alligator Alcatraz" as the name.<ref name="Bridges 07082025">{{Cite news|last=Bridges|first=C.A.|date=July 8, 2025|title=Is Alligator Alcatraz the official name of the Florida immigrant detention center?|newspaper=[[The Palm Beach Post]]|url=https://www.palmbeachpost.com/story/news/politics/2025/07/08/alligator-alcatraz-official-name-florida-immigrant-detention/84502452007/|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250714035901/https://www.palmbeachpost.com/story/news/politics/2025/07/08/alligator-alcatraz-official-name-florida-immigrant-detention/84502452007/|url-status=dead|archive-date=July 14, 2025|access-date=August 30, 2025|quote="Alligator Alcatraz" is official.}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|date=July 6, 2025|title=Alligator Alcatraz has opened in the Florida Everglades. Here are some takeaways|newspaper=[[Miami Herald]]|url=https://www.miamiherald.com/news/local/immigration/article309976110.html|url-access=subscription|access-date=August 30, 2025}}</ref> The Florida Division of Emergency Management and the governor's office bypassed procurement and competitive bidding rules to rapidly install the site. Private companies, many who donated to Republican candidates, obtained no-bid contracts to set up the camp.<ref name="Ellenbogen"/><ref name="Bob-Norman"/> [[Florida International University]] employees were instructed to covertly deliver university-owned equipment on June 27.<ref name="Martinez">{{cite news |last=Martinez |first=Alexandra  |date=2025-08-11 |title=FIU workers were directed to secretly deliver equipment to ‘Alligator Alcatraz’  |url=https://prismreports.org/2025/08/11/fiu-workers-secretly-deliver-equipment-to-alligator-alcatraz/|work=Prism}}</ref> 

IRG Global Emergency Management, who had given $10,000 to Florida's Republican Party on June 24, 2025, was awarded a $1.1 million contract for operational support services, followed by two more contracts at the Ochopee site.<ref name="Ellenbogen">Ellenbogen, Romy (July 12, 2025) [https://www.miamiherald.com/news/politics-government/article310522645.html#storylink=cpy Company's Alligator Alcatraz contracts followed donation to the Florida GOP] ''[[Miami Herald]]''. retrieved August 14, 2025.</ref> IRG is an offshoot of Access Restoration Services US, Inc., a major campaign donor to DeSantis and totaling nearly $400,000 in donations to Republican coffers.<ref name="Bob-Norman">Bob Norman, Bob & DeMarco, Michelle (July 4, 2025)  [https://www.orlandoweekly.com/news/big-desantis-campaign-donor-set-to-reap-millions-from-alligator-alcatraz-detention-camp-39884579 Big DeSantis campaign donor set to reap millions from 'Alligator Alcatraz' detention camp]. ''[[Orlando Weekly]]''. Retrieved August 14, 2025.</ref> The Critical Response Strategies (CRS) company initially received a $78 million no-bid contract from Florida emergency funds for staffing and some communications with lawyers.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Brigida  |first1=Anna-Catherine |last2=Monroe |first2= Nate |title=Jacksonville firm with $78 million ‘Alligator Alcatraz’ contract has obscure origins  |url=https://floridatrib.org/2025/07/16/jacksonville-firm-with-78-million-alligator-alcatraz-contract-has-obscure-origins/ |access-date=8 September 2025 |work=FloridaTrib |date=16 July 2025}}</ref><ref>Schlosser, Eric. (June 4, 2026). [https://www.theatlantic.com/ideas/2026/06/alligator-alcatraz-desantis-florida-immigration/687415/ The Alligator Alcatraz Boondoggle.] ''[[The Atlantic]]''</ref>  Carlos Duart, president of CDR Companies, formaly CDR Maguire, and Tina Vidal-Duart had donated $1.9 million to the Republican Party of Florida and two political action committees supporting DeSantis when the company was contracted, without bidding, for site construction.<ref name="CDR Companies"/> CDR Enterprises also made a $250,000 donation to Friends of James Uthmeier on Sept. 17, 2025, on top of a previous $25,000 contribution.<ref name="Uthmeier"/> CDR Health, run by Tina Vidal-Duart, was also awarded $17.5 million for its role in the facility, according to the Florida Accountability and Contract Tracking System (FACTS).<ref name="Martinez"/> 

During the opening press conference on July 1, 2025, Trump and Noem joined DeSantis, ICE Director Todd Lyons, FDEM Director Kevin Gutherie and other Florida officials.<ref name="CDR Companies"/> After migrants arrived on July 3, the press was forbidden to enter the site. Trump said the compound "might be as good as the real Alcatraz," adding it's "a little controversial, but I couldn't care less."<ref name="NBC_News">{{cite news |last1=Dixon |first1=Matt |last2=Gutierrez |first2=Gabe |date=2025-07-01 |title='Alligator Alcatraz' immigrant detention facility opens, with Trump in attendance |url=https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/donald-trump/alligator-alcatraz-set-open-trump-desantis-rcna215943|publisher=[[NBC News]]|archive-date=July 1, 2025 |access-date=July 1, 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250701195911/https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/donald-trump/alligator-alcatraz-set-open-trump-desantis-rcna215943 |url-status=live }}</ref> Desantis repeated in July 2025 that all detainees had a final removal order, which Eunice Cho of the ACLU stated is "clearly inaccurate."<ref name="auto6">Putterman, Samantha; Ramirez Uribe, Maria. (July 30, 2025) [https://www.politifact.com/article/2025/jul/30/DeSantis-Alligator-Alcatraz-deportation-order/. DeSantis said ‘everybody’ at Alligator Alcatraz has a deportation order. Lawyers say he’s wrong.] ''[[PolitiFact]]''.</ref>

===Moniker===
The moniker alludes to both the local [[American alligator]] population and the former maximum-security [[Alcatraz Federal Penitentiary]]. In American slang, [[alligator bait]] or gator bait is a [[racial slur]] for African Americans, implying they are worthless and expendable. Whatever the intentions, the moniker echoes a long tradition of using alligators in ways that have reinforced racist imagery and dehumanizing stereotypes according to Historian Mark V. Barrow, Jr. of [[Virginia Tech]].<ref>{{Cite news|last1=Barrow Jr.|first1=Mark V. |date=August 12, 2026|title=The forgotten racial history of Alligator Alcatraz|newspaper=[[Miami Herald]]|url=https://www.wlrn.org/immigration/2026-08-13/the-forgotten-racial-history-of-alligator-alcatraz|access-date=August 16, 2026}}</ref> In 1919 the Florida Department of Agriculture and Florida State Live Stock Association explicitly discouraged any references to "alligators lying in wait for [[pickaninny|pickaninnies]]", describing them as harmful for the image of the state and against the commercial interests of its citizens.{{sfnp|Hughes|2017}} In 2020, the [[University of Florida]] decided to end the [[Gator Bait chant|"Gator Bait" chant]] during athletic events due to "horrific racist imagery" associated with the phrase.{{sfnp|Van Ness|2020}} The high-security Alcatraz Federal Penitentiary housed convicted criminals and was by far the most expensive prison in the United States, and many still perceived it as America’s most extreme jail.{{sfn|Dunbar|1999|p=14}}

=== "The box" cage ===
[[File:OIG-26-22 Figure 12. Small Metal Enclosure.jpg|thumb|Small metal cage, nicknamed "the box"]]
Within weeks of its opening, a Nicaraguan migrant seeking U.S. asylum reported to WLRN that guards put him into what they called [[Box (torture)|"the box"]]<ref name="auto11"/>, a four-by-four-foot square enclosure outside in the sun and heat, for several hours, with no water and his hands and feet painfully shackled.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Padgett |first=Tim |date=2025-07-22 |title='They chained me to the ground': Detainees at Alligator Alcatraz allege harsh punishment by guards|url=https://www.wlrn.org/immigration/2025-07-22/alligator-alcatraz-detainee-punishments|access-date=2026-10-03|publisher=[[WLRN-FM]]|language=en-US}}</ref> Rebecca Sharpless, director of the Immigration Clinic at the [[University of Miami]], confirmed a similar account from a young man shackled in an outside cage the size of a vending machine.<ref name="healyNdonwie">{{Cite news |last=Healy |first=Claire |last2=Ndonwie |first2=Churchill |date=2026-09-20 |title=Former Alligator Alcatraz detainees dispute ‘punishment box’ depiction |url=https://www.tampabay.com/news/florida/2026/09/17/former-alligator-alcatraz-detainees-dispute-punishment-box-depiction//|newspaper=[[Naples Daily News]]|language=en-US}}</ref> Such practices are associated with the death of [[Marcia Powell]] at the [[Arizona State Prison Complex – Perryville]]. In March 2026, Senators [[Jon Ossoff]] and [[Dick Durbin]], Senate Minority Whip and ranking member of the Senate Judiciary Committee, initiated an investigation of the use of shackles and 'the box'.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Foster |first=Kyle J.|date=2026-04-06 |title='The box' at Alligator Alcatraz called a torture device. What we know |url=https://eu.naplesnews.com/story/news/local/2026/04/06/the-box-at-alligator-alcatraz-called-a-torture-device-under-investigation-what-we-know/89448454007//|work=Naples Daily News |language=en-US}}</ref> [[Amnesty International]] denounced the camp's cruel, inhuman and degrading treatment, including the use of the ‘box’ in December 2025.<ref name="auto3">{{cite web |title=Torture and Enforced Disappearances in the Sunshine State: Human Rights Violations at "Alligator Alcatraz" and Krome in Florida |url=https://www.amnestyusa.org/reports/torture-and-enforced-disappearances-in-the-sunshine-state-human-rights-violations-at-alligator-alcatraz-and-krome-in-florida/|publisher=[[Amnesty International USA]]|date=December 4, 2025}}</ref> In September 2026, the Inspector General of the Department of Homeland Security Office confirmed the practice of guards placing people in  4 x 4 foot outdoor metal cages at the camp and at other sites in South Florida.<ref name="Shockey 09142026"/> 

=== Runway ===
[[File:JET TAKES OFF FROM MIAMI-DADE JETPORT IN EVERGLADES - NARA - 544491.jpg|thumb|Takeoff of an airplane at the Everglades Jetport, July 1972]]
DeSantis said the airstrip would serve as a "one-stop" shop using the on-site runway<ref name="Lowery 102425">{{Cite news |last=Lowery |first=Kairi |date=2026-07-17 |title=Built in a flash: new satellite imagery shows rapid construction of 'Alligator Alcatraz'|url=https://www.wuft.org/fresh-take-florida/2025-10-24/built-in-a-flash-new-satellite-imagery-shows-rapid-construction-of-alligator-alcatraz|access-date=2025-10-24|publisher=[[WUFT (TV)|WUFT]]|language=en-US}}</ref> for deportation. Data from the ''[[Miami Herald]]'' and ''[[Tampa Bay Times]]'' show it was used as a holding pen and transfer hub for immigrants still fighting their cases in immigration courts.<ref>Wieder, Ben; Ceballos, Ana. (Updated June 17, 2026) [https://www.miamiherald.com/news/local/immigration/article311718011.html ‘Psychological warfare’: Internal data shows true nature of Alligator Alcatraz]. ''[[Miami Herald]]''.</ref> State officials said deportation flights began immediately after opening with a “surge” of immigration arrests, an ICE spokesperson answering, “Fire up the deportation planes.” <ref>Sayers, Devon; Rosales, Isabel.(July 25, 2025) [https://edition.cnn.com/2025/07/25/us/alligator-alcatraz-deportation-flights Deportation flights from ‘Alligator Alcatraz’ begin as Florida vows a ‘surge’ of immigration arrests.] [[CNN]].</ref> Flights included shuffle flights (in between US facilities), removal flights to a foreign country, and removal related flights (fuel stops and connections), with 50 such flights in 2025 and 108 flights between January and May 2026.<ref>Human Rights First. (June 2026) [https://www.humanrightsfirst.org/library/ice-flight-monitor-may-2026-report Ice Flight Monitor June 2026 Report. See: Ochopee on page 27. Nationally, there were 13,962 such flights in 2025.].</ref> Shuffle flights increased in June 2026.<ref>Chavez, Juan Carlos. (May 23, 2026) [https://www.tampabay.com/news/florida-politics/2026/05/22/alligator-alcatraz-transfers-immigration-detention-closing-florida/ Lawyers say Alligator Alcatraz detainee transfers are ramping up.] ''[[Tampa Bay Times]]''.</ref> Court documents note deportations from the center included noncitizens of Mexico transported to the Mexican border, although Mexico refused their legal entry.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://ecf.flmd.uscourts.gov/cgi-bin/show_public_doc?2026-01258-12-2-cv|author=Steele, John E.|title=Opinion and Order, ''Fredy Hernandez Espinosa v. Warden, Florida Soft Side Detention Center, et al.'', Case No. 2:26-cv-1258-JES-DNF|publisher=[[United States District Court, Middle District of Florida]], [[Fort Myers]] Division|language=en-US|url-status=live|date=June 10, 2026|access-date=November 1, 2026|archive-date=November 1, 2026|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20261101201125/https://ecf.flmd.uscourts.gov/cgi-bin/show_public_doc?2026-01258-12-2-cv}}</ref><ref>Walker, Heather; Hall, Darcelle. (May 5, 2026) [https://wsvn.com/news/investigations/detainee-at-alligator-alcatraz-says-us-officials-took-him-to-mexican-border-without-paperwork-approval-from-mexican-authorities/ Detainee at ‘Alligator Alcatraz’ says US officials took him to Mexican border without paperwork, approval from Mexican authorities.] [[7News Miami]].</ref>

=== Closure ===
On June 16, 2026, DHS officials indicated that all detainees had been transferred to undisclosed locations.<ref>{{Cite news |last1=Krueger |first1=Kristi |last2=Forney |first2=Terrell |date=2026-06-16 |title=All detainees moved out of 'Alligator Alcatraz'|url=https://www.local10.com/news/local/2026/06/16/all-detainees-moved-out-of-alligator-alcatraz/|publisher=[[WPLG]] |language=en-US}}</ref> Florida Emergency Management Director Kevin Guthrie instructed [[Controversies involving ICE and private businesses|private businesses]] to remove tents, fences, trailers and other structures from the site, thus initiating a "full demobilization" of the facility<ref>{{Cite news |last1=Ovalle |first1=David |last2=Mazzei |first2=Patricia |date=2026-06-23 |title=Vendors Told to Start Dismantling Florida's 'Alligator Alcatraz' Detention Center |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2026/06/23/us/alligator-alcatraz-closing.html|newspaper=[[The New York Times]]|language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}}</ref><ref name=NBCNews6.22.26/> and leaving 20 acres of asphalt added without permit to the original 35 acres.<ref name="Ryan 071726">{{Cite news |last=Ryan |first=Alexa |date=2026-07-17 |title=Alligator Alcatraz gates closed: What's next for environmental groups?|url=https://eu.naplesnews.com/story/news/local/2026/07/13/alligator-alcatraz-sign-taken-down-gates-locked-whats-next/90906686007/ |access-date=2026-07-18 |work=Naples Daily News|language=en-US}}</ref><ref name="Lowery 102425"/> Following this declaration, Miami-Dade Mayor Daniella Levine Cava said her administration would explore transferring county-owned land at the site to the [[National Park Service]] or other Everglades restoration partners.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.france24.com/en/americas/20260625-florida-s-alligator-alcatraz-detention-center-shuts-down-says-official|title=Trump's 'Alligator Alcatraz' immigration detention centre closes after less than a year]|publisher=[[France24]]|language=en|url-status=live|date=June 25, 2026|access-date=November 1, 2026|archive-date=September 23, 2026|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260923024547/https://www.france24.com/en/americas/20260625-florida-s-alligator-alcatraz-detention-center-shuts-down-says-official}}</ref> In July 2026, a federal judge requested proof from DeSantis that the camp was closed in the context of a lawsuit brought by the American Civil Liberties Union's National Prison Project.<ref name="Mayet 071626">{{Cite news|last=Mayat|first=Stephany|date=2026-07-16|title=Federal judge asks: Is 'Alligator Alcatraz' really closed?|url=https://eu.tallahassee.com/story/news/state/2026/07/16/judge-demands-proof-alligator-alcatraz-is-actually-closed/90941921007/|access-date=2026-07-17|work=[[Tallahassee Democrat]]|language=en-US}}</ref>

According to the Amendment filed by Friends of the Everglades on August 12, 2026, the interventions on site continue after shuttering to cause direct and indirect harm to the wetlands, wildlife, and air and water quality through lighting, noise, vehicle traffic, pollution, fencing, paving, demobilization activities, and other wildlife habitat disturbances, which degrade the natural, scenic, hydrologic, floral, and faunal, and recreational values of the area (see: Friends of the Everglades, Inc. v. Mullin).

==Detainees==
{{Infobox court case
| name = C.M. v. Noem
| court = [[Middle District of Florida]]
| full name = C.M., Michael Borrego Fernandez, J.M.C., E.R. on behalf of themselves and all others similarly situated v. | judge = [[Sheri Polster Chappell]]
| start date = {{Start date and age|2025|7|16}}

| appealed to =

| keywords = {{Hlist|[[First Amendment]]|[[Fifth Amendment to the United States Constitution|Fifth Amendment]]}}
| italic title = no
| docket = [https://clearinghouse.net/case/46799/ 2:25-cv-00747]

According to ICE data as of April 2026, the center held nearly 1,400 detainees, all men, and two-thirds of those detained were classified as noncriminal.<ref name="Closing"/> The first group of detainees arrived on July 3, 2025.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Anderson|first1=Curt|last2=Payne|first2=Kate|title=First immigration detainees arrive at Florida center in the Everglades|url=https://apnews.com/article/alligator-alcatraz-immigration-detainees-florida-56670910db4c88800d9df42ac3ce7f91|publisher=[[Associated Press]]|language=en-US|date=3 July 2025|access-date=November 1, 2026|archive-date=November 1, 2026|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20261101195401/https://apnews.com/article/alligator-alcatraz-immigration-detainees-florida-56670910db4c88800d9df42ac3ce7f91}}</ref> Director Kerner testified that "detainees were there solely on immigration violations, none on state criminal charges."<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://storage.courtlistener.com/recap/gov.uscourts.flsd.692544/gov.uscourts.flsd.692544.131.0_1.pdf|title=CASE NO. 25-22896-CV-WILLIAMS|publisher=[[Court Listener]]}}</ref> A review of official records revealed that people detained at the facility included [[Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals]] recipients<ref>Luciano, Lilia (August 12, 2025) [https://www.cbsnews.com/news/alligator-alcatraz-detainees-daca/ "Some 'Alligator Alcatraz' detainees are DACA recipients and have no criminal history, despite Trump's 'worst of the worst' claims"]. ''[[CBS Evening News]]''. Retrieved 14 August 2025.</ref> and persons on student visas, including Hari Koneru from [[India]] whose lawyer Anna Weiser declared he does not have an order of removal.<ref name="auto6"/>

Detained people have included husbands of US citizens, including those seeking asylum or attending [[United States Citizenship and Immigration Services]] greencard interviews.<ref>Mena, Kelly. (May 5, 2026) [https://ny1.com/nyc/all-boroughs/politics/2026/05/05/brooklyn-couple-reunited-ice-detention- "Brooklyn couple reunited after ICE detainment"]. [[Spectrum News]], New York.</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nbcmiami.com/news/local/alligator-alcatraz-immigation-detention-center-closure/3808365/|title=Detainees will move out of 'Alligator Alcatraz,' facility to shut down by June, source says|publisher=[[Associated Press]]|via=[[NBC6 South Florida]]|language=en-US|url-status=live|date=May 12, 2026|access-date=November 1, 2026|archive-date=May 12, 2026|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260512230653/https://www.nbcmiami.com/news/local/alligator-alcatraz-immigation-detention-center-closure/3808365/}}</ref> Also detained were fathers of US citizen children,<ref>Burke, Garance; Sonia Perez D. (June 4, 2026) [https://www.nbcwashington.com/news/national-international/trump-administration-separated-dozens-of-children-from-their-parents-for-a-second-time-ap-finds/4112405/ Trump administration separated dozens of children from their parents for a second time, AP finds]. ''4 NBC Washington''.</ref> including those with a greencard<ref name="auto">Mordowanec, Nick. (July 29, 2025) [https://www.newsweek.com/immigration-green-card-migrant-alligator-alcatraz-2105665 Man With Green Card for 25 Years in Alligator Alcatraz Has Hearing Canceled]. ''[[Newsweek]]''.</ref> or a current or expired [[Temporary Protected Status]].<ref>Ortiz Blanes, Syra. (May 29, 2026) [https://www.miamiherald.com/news/local/immigration/article315926108.html Trump administration deported Florida Keys man with TPS to Haiti. He’s back in the U.S.] ''[[Miami Herald]]''.</ref><ref>Taylor, Ivan. (December 18, 2025) [https://www.cbsnews.com/miami/news/legal-option-tps-holders-deportation-detentions-south-florida-alligator-alcatraz/ New legal option may help some TPS holders avoid deportation as detentions continue in South Florida]. [[CBS News]].</ref><ref>Michaels, Samantha. (July–August 2026) [https://www.motherjones.com/politics/2026/06/trump-family-separations-data-us-citizens-children-immigrant-parents-ice-obama-biden-policies/. ICE Took Mom and Dad. Now the Perez Kids Are Home Alone.] ''[[Mother Jones (magazine)|Mother Jones]]''.</ref> Justo Betancourt, the Cuban single father of US citizen, Arianne, spokesperson of [[The Workers Circle]], which organised the weekly vigils outside the gates <ref>The Workers Circle. [https://www.circle.org/freedom-vigils Freedom Vigils]</ref><ref>Morel, Laura C. (March 4, 2026) [https://www.motherjones.com/politics/2026/03/alligator-alcatraz-immigrant-detention-ice-florida-oppoition-she-quit-her-job-to-fight-for-her-fathers-freedomand-for-everyone-else/ She Quit Her Job to Fight for Her Father's Freedom—and for Everyone Else Inside Alligator Alcatraz.] ''[[Mother Jones (magazine)|Mother Jones]]''.</ref> was released  after six months of detention when his attorneys proved he was wrongfully detained.<ref name="auto8">Foster, J. Kyle. (May 15, 2026) [https://eu.naplesnews.com/story/news/local/2026/05/15/cuban-born-miami-resident-justo-betancourt-freed-from-alligator-alcatraz/90085075007/ Relieved daughter of Alligator Alcatraz detainee gets her dad back]. ''Fort Myers News-Press & Naples Daily News''.</ref> He was congratulated for his release by Trump.<ref>Durkee, Alison.  (June 1, 2026) [https://www.forbes.com/sites/alisondurkee/2026/06/01/trump-cheers-justo-betancourts-release-from-trumps-alligator-alcatraz-sparking-confusion/. Trump Cheers Justo Betancourt’s Release From Trump’s Alligator Alcatraz—Sparking Confusion.] ''[[Forbes]]''.</ref>

According to a list of the population obtained by the ''[[Tampa Bay Times]]'' and ''[[Miami Herald]]'' in mid-July, more than 95% of the detainees held at the site originated from Latin American countries. Approximately 20% of the population are Guatemalan citizens, ~20% Mexican citizens, and another ~10% Cuban citizens.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Ceballos |first1=Ana |last2=Healy|first2=Clair |last3=Dasgupta|first3=Dasgupta|last4=Wieder|first4=Ben|title=Some Alligator Alcatraz detainees have no criminal record, list shows |url=https://www.tampabay.com/news/florida/2025/07/13/some-alligator-alcatraz-detainees-have-no-criminal-record-list-shows/|newspaper=[[Tampa Bay Times]]|date=13 July 2025}}</ref> The ''New York Times'' reported that non-citizens from [[Cuba]] have been detained at the camp and deported at record numbers, including those seeking the [[right of asylum]].<ref>Mazzei, Patricia (January 19, 2026) "[https://www.nytimes.com/2026/01/19/us/politics/cubans-florida-deportations-trump.html?unlocked_article_code=1.F1A.8D6A.5CkALLy21VK9&smid=url-share Cubans in Florida Are Being Deported in Record Numbers]"</ref> [[Green card]] holder Douglas Dixon, one of at least two [[Canada|Canadians]] detained at the camp, declared, "They're treating people like animals. Alligator Alcatraz is like [[Nazi Germany|(Nazi) Germany]] in 1939, updated with 2026 rules."<ref>Trinh, Judy (April 15, 2026). [https://www.ctvnews.ca/canada/article/canadian-detained-at-alligator-alcatraz-for-owing-us12000-in-back-taxes/ Canadian living in Florida detained by ICE, sent to infamous 'Alligator Alcatraz']. ''CTVNEWS''.</ref> [[South Africa]]n of TV reality show and former lawyer, Peet Viljoen, who previously praised Trump and echoed claims about so-called “[[White genocide conspiracy theory|white genocide]]” in South Africa, was detained on a charge of aggravated grand retail theft and later transferred to the [[California City Correctional Facility|California City Detention Facility]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Selisho |first=Kaunda |date=2026-04-10 |title=RHOP's Mel and Peet Viljoen plead 'not guilty' in Florida retail theft case |url=https://www.citizen.co.za/lifestyle/entertainment/celebrity-news/rhops-mel-and-peet-viljoen-plead-not-guilty/ |access-date=2026-06-25 |website=The Citizen |language=en}}</ref><ref>Kwazi, Thami. (12 May 2026) [https://www.citizen.co.za/lifestyle/entertainment/peet-viljoen-turns-on-trump-compares-ice-centre-to-hitlers-auschwitz-on-steroids/ Peet Viljoen turns on Trump, compares ICE centre to ‘Hitler’s Auschwitz on steroids'] ''The Citizen''.</ref>

In October 2025, The ''[[Miami Herald]]'',<ref>{{cite news |last1=Wieder |first1=Ben |last2=Dasgupta |first2=Shirsho |title=Hundreds of Alligator Alcatraz detainees drop off the grid after leaving site |url=https://www.miamiherald.com/news/local/immigration/article312042943.html|newspaper=[[Miami Herald]]|date=15 September 2025}}</ref> as well as detainees' family and lawyers,<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.boredpanda.com/two-thirds-of-detainees-alligator-alcantaraz-are-missing/ |title=Hundreds Of Detainees Reportedly Missing From ICE Records After Being Sent To 'Alligator Alcatraz'|website=[[Bored Panda]]|date=September 29, 2025|access-date=November 1, 2026|archive-date=October 7, 2025|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251007090917/https://www.boredpanda.com/two-thirds-of-detainees-alligator-alcantaraz-are-missing/}}</ref> reported that the whereabouts of about two-thirds of over 1,800 detainees held at the facility in July could not be determined.<ref name="guardian"/> The average stay of the 21,000 persons detained on site was 16 days.<ref name="auto2"/>

==Court-ordered release or bond hearing==
===Court-ordered immediate release===
On April 1, 2026, Judge [[Sheri Polster Chappell]] of the US District Court of the Fort Myers Division ordered the immediate release of Noel Traba Ramirez, who had filed for asylum from Cuba, esteeming that "ICE clearly exceeded its statutory authority when it designated him for expedited removal."<ref name="auto4"/> Following his petition for Writ of [[Habeas Corpus]], Judge Polster Chappell ordered, on April 9, 2026, the immediate release of Jose Alberto Molina, a native of Cuba who was paroled into the United States in 2004.<ref>Molina v. Warden, ALLIGATOR ALCATRAZ et al. (April 9, 2026) [https://ecf.flmd.uscourts.gov/cgi-bin/show%20public%20doc?2026-00380-7-2-cv Case No.: 2:26-cv-00380-SPC-DNF] (M.D. Fla. 2026) [[United States District Court, Middle District of Florida]], [[Fort Myers]] Division</ref> U.S. District Judge [[Kyle Dudek]] also referred to Habeas Corpus when ordering Justo Betancourt's release from ICE custody within 48 hours on May 13, 2026.<ref name="auto8"/> On May 15, 2026, Adrian Cambara Ortiz, originally from Cuba, was also immediately released by the United States District Court, Middle District of Florida, Fort Myers Division, after five months of detention.<ref>[https://cases.justia.com/federal/district-courts/florida/flmdce/2:2026cv01363/458688/8/0.pdfl. Adrian Cambara Ortiz v. Warden, Florida Soft Side Detention Center et al.] (May 15, 2026). [[United States District Court, Middle District of Florida]], [[Fort Myers]] Division.</ref>

Senior United States Judge John E. Steele ordered the immediate release on May 18, 2026 of the Cuban-born Jose Miguel Bello Valdez and of Gabriel Antonio Perez Romero, on June 3, 2026, citing their refusal of deportation to Mexico and the US Supreme Court case [[Zadvydas v. Davis]].<ref>[https://ecf.flmd.uscourts.gov/cgi-bin/show_public_doc?2026-01340-9-2-cv Jose Miguel Bello Valdez v. Warden, Florida Soft Side Detention Center, et al.] (May 18, 2026) [[United States District Court, Middle District of Florida]], [[Fort Myers]] Division.</ref> The Cuban-born Gabriel Antonio Perez Romero was initially detained in November 2025 by ICE during a regularly scheduled reporting appointment and taken to the [[San Ysidro, San Diego]] port of entry in January 2026, before court-ordered release.<ref>[https://ecf.flmd.uscourts.gov/cgi-bin/show_public_doc?2026-00012-17-2-cv Gabriel Antonio Perez Romero v. Warden, Florida Soft Side Detention Center, et al.] (June 3, 2026) [[United States District Court, Middle District of Florida]], [[Fort Myers]] Division.</ref> Of Cuban origin, Ricardo Rodriguez refused to cross the Mexican border in February and April 2026, before court-ordered release in June 2026.<ref>[https://ecf.flmd.uscourts.gov/cgi-bin/show_public_doc?2026-01758-8-2-cv Ricardo Rodriguez v. Warden, Florida Soft Side Detention Center, et al.] (June 10, 2026) [[United States District Court, Middle District of Florida]], [[Fort Myers]] Division. Case No.: 2:26-cv-01758-SPC-KRH.</ref>

When ordering the immediate release of Alejandro Osvaldo Ghysels Reales, a recipient of a [[U visa]] for victims of crimes (and their immediate family members) who have suffered substantial mental or physical abuse while in the U.S. and who are willing to assist law enforcement and government officials, U.S. District Judge Kyle C. Cohen noted, “The Government simply scooped up a man protected by an active grant of deferred action, locked him in a cell, and submitted a brief to this Court that pretends the protection does not exist".<ref>Vasquez, Wendy. (April 23, 2026) [https://www.tampafp.com/florida-judge-slams-ice-for-alligator-alcatraz-detention-of-man-shielded-from-deportation/ Florida Judge Slams ICE For ‘Alligator Alcatraz’ Detention Of Man Shielded From Deportation]. ''Tampa Free Press''.</ref>

===Bond hearings===
On July 23, 2025, the bond hearing of green card holder and U.S. permanent resident since 2000, Gonzalo Almanza, father of an 8-year old US citizen, was abruptly cancelled without notice, a pattern reportedly affecting other detainees.<ref name="auto"/> On May 11, 2026, U.S. District Judge Dudek found that plaintif Omar Felipe Suarez Reye is not entitled to immediate release but is entitled to a bond hearing for release.<ref>Suarez Reyes v. Matthew Mordant, Florida Soft Side Dentention Center, et al. (May 11, 2026) [https://ecf.flmd.uscourts.gov/cgi-bin/show%20public%20doc?2026-01218-9-2-cv Case No. 2:26-cv-1218-KCD-NPM]. [[United States District Court, Middle District of Florida]], [[Fort Myers]] Division.</ref> On May 13, 2026, Tomas Rubio Rincon, who arrived from Mexico over twenty years ago, was ordered to be immediately released or granted a bond hearing within ten days for release, in accordance with the [[Immigration and Nationality Act]].<ref>[https://law.justia.com/cases/federal/district-courts/florida/flmdce/2:2026cv01344/458516/11/ Tomas Rubio Rincon v. Garrett Ripa et al.] (May 13, 2026). [[United States District Court, Middle District of Florida]], [[Fort Myers]] Division.</ref>

Vargas Sergi lawfully entered the US from [[Venezuela]] in 2015 and applied for asylum in 2016. Married and the father of two children, he has an authorization to work. ICE arrested him in April 2026 and an immigration judge denied his release during a bond hearing citing traffic tickets, a possible boat-registration issue and a "danger to the community". A court ordered his immediate release in June 2026 judging that he is neither a flight risk, nor a danger to the community.<ref>[https://ecf.flmd.uscourts.gov/cgi-bin/show_public_doc?2026-01732-12-2-cv Vargas Sergi v. Warden, Florida Soft Side Detention Center, et al.] (June 9, 2026) [[United States District Court, Middle District of Florida]], [[Fort Myers]] DivisionN. Case No.: 2:26-cv-01732-SPC-NPM.</ref>

==Reports of inhumane treatment==
Detainees reported harsh conditions at the facility, citing limited access to water, insufficient food, and restrictions on the practice of their religion.<ref>{{cite news |last1=McAllister |first1=Anna |title=Alligator Alcatraz detainees allege inhumane conditions at immigration detention center |url=https://www.cbsnews.com/miami/news/alligator-alcatraz-detainees-allege-inhumane-conditions-at-immigration-detention-center/ |access-date=9 July 2025|publisher=[[CBS News]]|date=8 July 2025}}</ref> Detainees have described unsanitary conditions, including wastewater overflows and insect infestations, as well as inadequate access to medical care.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Salomon |first1=Gisela |last2=Payne |first2=Kate |title=Detained immigrants at 'Alligator Alcatraz' say there are worms in food and wastewater on the floor |url=https://apnews.com/article/alligator-alcatraz-immigration-detainees-florida-cc2fb9e34e760a50e97f13fe59cbf075|publisher=[[Associated Press]]|language=en-US|date=11 July 2025|access-date=November 1, 2026|archive-date=July 11, 2025|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250711191840/https://apnews.com/article/alligator-alcatraz-immigration-detainees-florida-cc2fb9e34e760a50e97f13fe59cbf075}}</ref> The area on which the facility is located is also subject to frequent bouts of extreme weather, including [[List of Florida hurricanes (2000–present)|yearly hurricanes]], heavy rainfall, and high heat.<ref>{{Cite news |last1=Tabuchi |first1=Hiroko |last2=Rojanasakul |first2=Mira |date=2025-08-04 |title=Environmental Concerns at 'Alligator Alcatraz' Include Storms and Flooding |url=https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2025/08/04/climate/alligator-alcatraz-hurricanes-storms.html|access-date=2025-08-04|newspaper=[[The New York Times]]|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331}}</ref>

On July 21, ''[[The Guardian]]'' described the facility, as well as Krome and a Miami jail, as being at the center of "a succession of alleged abuses at jails operated by Immigration and Customs Enforcement Agency (ICE) in the state since January, chronicled by the advocacy groups [[Human Rights Watch]], Americans for Immigrant Justice, and Sanctuary of the South from interviews with detainees".<ref>{{Cite news|last=Luscombe|first=Richard|date=July 21, 2025|title=Migrants at Ice jail in Miami made to kneel to eat 'like dogs', report alleges|newspaper=[[The Guardian]]|language=en-GB|url=https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2025/jul/21/migrants-miami-ice-jail-abuses|access-date=August 29, 2025}}</ref> A month later, the outlet described reports of inhumane treatment and brutality at the camp as being commonplace.<ref name="Luscombe 08292025"/>

On July 22, people detained on site began a [[hunger strike]] to protest what they consider to be inhumane and dangerous living conditions.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2025-08-01 |title='Alligator Alcatraz' detainees on hunger strike for 10th day, protesting conditions |url=https://www.nbcnews.com/news/latino/alligator-alcatraz-hunger-strike-detainees-protest-conditions-rcna222554|access-date=2025-08-04|publisher=[[NBC News]]|language=en-US}}</ref> Some detainees reported maggots in the food and having to "dig the fecal matter out of the toilets with their bare hands" for lack of plumbing. The Florida Division of Emergency Management has denied the claims, but no independent inspections have been allowed.<ref>{{cite web|author=Quinn, Allison|url=https://nymag.com/intelligencer/article/alligator-alcatraz-conditions-mass-deportation-prison-model.html|title='Alligator Alcatraz' Is Worse Than You Realize Kristi Noem calls it a 'model' prison. Domnioes she know about the maggots?|website=[[Intelligencer (website)|Intelligencer]]|date=August 7, 2025|access-date=November 1, 2026|archive-date=March 5, 2026|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260305103821/https://nymag.com/intelligencer/article/alligator-alcatraz-conditions-mass-deportation-prison-model.html}}</ref>

On August 29, three detainees said an uprising occurred at the facility in phone calls to Miami's Spanish language news channel Noticias 23. The incident allegedly occurred after several detainees shouted "freedom" after one received news a relative had died. The detainees described guards as indiscriminately beating detainees with batons and firing tear gas. The Florida Division of Emergency Management denied reports that the events had occurred.<ref name="Luscombe 08292025">{{Cite news|last=Luscombe|first=Richard|date=August 29, 2025|title=Detainees report alleged uprising at 'Alligator Alcatraz': 'A lot of people have bled'|newspaper=[[The Guardian]]|language=en-GB|url=https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2025/aug/29/alligator-alcatraz-uprising-florida-immigration|access-date=August 29, 2025|quote=Reports of 'inhumane' conditions and brutality at the camp, where migrants are held in metal cages as they await deportation, have become commonplace.}}</ref>

In December 2025, the report "Torture and Enforced Disappearances in the Sunshine State: Human Rights Violations at 'Alligator Alcatraz' and Krome in Florida" published by [[Amnesty International]] concluded that the camp's conditions, including routine and prolonged use of shackles and retention in a [[box (torture)|"box"]] described as a cage-like structure "constitutes [[torture]]".<ref name="auto3"/>

In 2026, an investigation over reports of abuse at the [[Everglades]] tent facility was filed by [[U.S. Senators]] [[Jon Ossoff]] of [[Georgia (U.S. state)|Georgia]] and [[Dick Durbin]] of [[Illinois]], focusing on allegations of [[torture]].<ref>Churchill, Ndonwie (28 March 2026) [https://www.pressreader.com/usa/the-union-democrat/20260328/281539412495811 'Senators launch probe into Alligator Alcatraz 'torture' allegations.'] ''[[The Union Democrat]]''.</ref> After an unannounced visit in April 2026, Congresswoman [[Debbie Wasserman Schultz]] stated, everything about this detention camp "screams inhumane and unnecessary."<ref>Bustos, Sergio R. (April 9, 2026). [https://www.wlrn.org/immigration/2026-04-09/florida-congresswoman-1-500-people-remain-housed-under-inhumane-conditions-at-alligator-alcatraz 'Florida congresswoman: 1,500 people remain housed under 'inhumane' conditions at Alligator Alcatraz'], [[WLRN South Florida]], [[BBC News]].</ref> Controversy continues related to possible federal funding<ref>Crawford, Jennifer (October 1, 2025) [https://www.wgcu.org/top-story/2025-10-02/environmental-group-media-report-confirms-feds-reimbursed-florida-for-detention-center "Federal reimbursement confirmed for detention center; environmental groups say info backs lawsuit claims."] [[WGCU (TV)|WGCU News]]. Retrieved October 28, 2025.</ref> for this first state-run facility within the context of [[immigration to the United States]] and [[List of deaths in ICE detention|deaths during ICE detention]].<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2025/08/21/us/alligator-alcatraz-florida-ruling.html |title=Judge Orders That 'Alligator Alcatraz' Detention Center Be Shut Down for Now|newspaper=[[The New York Times]]|access-date=September 19, 2025|date=August 21, 2025|first1=Patricia |last1=Mazzei |first2=David C. |last2=Adams}}</ref><ref>Heddles, Claire; Ndonwie, Churchill. (February 26, 2026) [https://www.tampabay.com/news/florida-politics/2026/02/25/alligator-alcatraz-federal-funding-reimbursement-trump-desantis-uthmeier/ Florida admits federal funding for Alligator Alcatraz may not come.] ''[[Miami Herald]]''.</ref>

The ''Miami Herald's'' review of one year of emergency calls to 911 by concerned family and friends detail a lack of medical attention within the camp and a lack of communication about medical emergencies.<ref name="auto9"/>

In September 2026, a DHS Office of Inspector General report said the site used "small metal enclosures" covering 18 square feet that presented "significant risks" to detainee's health and safety as "calming areas."<ref>{{cite news |last1=Ngo |first1=Madelene |last2=Aleaziz |first2=Hamed |last3=Ovalle |first3=David |title=‘Alligator Alcatraz’ Used Small Cages as ‘Calming Areas,’ Report Says |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/14/us/alligator-alcatraz-dhs-inspector-general.html |access-date=14 September 2026|newspaper=[[The New York Times]]|date=14 September 2026}}</ref>

==Construction and operational costs==
The total cost for the facility before dismantlement was estimated in June 2026 by [[CBS News Miami]] to be $1.2 billion or over $3,500 a day per detainee.<ref name="auto2">Defede, Jim (June 28, 2026) [https://www.cbsnews.com/miami/news/cbs-news-miami-investigates-the-cost-of-alligator-alcatraz-after-its-shutdown/ CBS News Miami investigates the cost of Alligator Alcatraz after its shutdown]. [[CBS News Miami]].</ref> According to the [[United States Government Accountability Office]], ICE neglected standard practice by not entering into a contract or intergovernmental service agreement or negotiate costs with the state of Florida for the camp, leading to high operating costs.<ref name="watchdog"/> Florida officials initially announced a cost of US$450 million a year to operate.<ref>Cooper, Julia (July 7, 2025). "[https://www.wlrn.org/news-in-brief/2025-07-07/miamis-first-cuban-born-mayor-speaks-out-against-alligator-alcatraz Miami's first Cuban-born Mayor speaks out against 'Alligator Alcatraz]'", [[WLRN-TV|WLRN]]. Retrieved August 6, 2025.</ref><ref>Ndonwie, Churchill (July 24, 2025) [https://www.miamiherald.com/news/local/immigration/article311075435.html "Contracts reveal the big business of building and operating Alligator Alcatraz"] ''[[Miami Herald]]''. Retrieved 7 August 2025.</ref> 

Documents requested by Second Judicial Circuit Judge Angela Dempsey in March 2026 showed Florida had spent more than $1.2 million per day to run the camp, with a daily [[burn rate]] of $3 million a day during its earliest weeks.<ref name=WGCU3.4.26>{{cite web|url=https://www.wgcu.org/investigation/2026-03-03/new-records-show-florida-officials-burned-more-than-1-2-million-per-day-on-alligator-alcatraz|title=New records show Florida officials burned more than $1.2 million per day on 'Alligator Alcatraz'|author=Payne, Kate|publisher=[[WGCU (TV)|WGCU News]]|language=en-US|url-status=live|date=March 4, 2026|access-date=November 1, 2026|archive-date=March 3, 2026|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260303175512/https://www.wgcu.org/investigation/2026-03-03/new-records-show-florida-officials-burned-more-than-1-2-million-per-day-on-alligator-alcatraz}}</ref> In July 2026, [[CBS News Miami]] calculated the average daily cost for the camp at $3.4 million.<ref>{{Cite news|last1=DeFede |first1=Jim|date=July 5, 2026|title=Florida's Attorney General faces new attacks over Alligator Alcatraz and Hope Florida|publisher=[[CBS News]]|url=https://www.cbsnews.com/miami/news/floridas-attorney-general-faces-new-attacks-over-alligator-alcatraz-and-hope-florida/}}</ref> 

Fewer than 70 [[Florida National Guard]] were on duty to guard the remote detention site.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Mitchell |first1=Ellen |title=About 70 National Guard troops activated to protect Alligator Alcatraz|url=https://thehill.com/policy/defense/5382393-national-guard-troops-activated-alligator-alcatraz/|date=July 2, 2025|newspaper=[[The Hill (newspaper)|The Hill]]}}</ref> The private company GardaWorld was hired for security. U.S. Representatives [[Greg Stanton]], [[Yassamin Ansari]] and [[Adelita Grijalva]] remain concerned that GardaWorld "does not appear to have experience constructing and operating immigration detention centers".<ref>{{cite news |last1=Gonzales |first1=Daniel |title=House Dems want answers on AZ immigration detention projects|url=https://tucson.com/news/state-regional/government-politics/article_1a49b232-e3ab-40a6-b9f3-5c70221e5645.html|date=October 8, 2026 |work=Arizona Daily Star}}</ref>

In early August 2025, the [[Federal Emergency Management Agency]] confirmed reception of a grant application from state officials, later evaluated as a US$1.49 billion grant.<ref name=WGCU3.4.26/> In August 15, federal officials provided the Florida Division of Emergency Management (FDEM) with instructions related to the use of US$608 million funds.<ref>FRIENDS OF THE EVERGLADES, INC., et al., v. EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR, FLORIDA DIVISION OF EMERGENCY MANAGEMENT, [https://earthjustice.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/01/2026-01-07-90-25-12873-time-sensitive-motion-for-excess-words_pages-.pdf Case No. 25-12873], Document 90, filed on 01/07/2026.</ref> As of August 29, 2025, the State of Florida had incurred $218 million of [[sunk costs]] for the construction of the facility.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://us.cnn.com/2025/08/29/us/alligator-alcatraz-shutdown-florida-financial-loss|title=Florida may lose $218 million on empty 'Alligator Alcatraz' as judge orders shutdown|date=August 29, 2025|publisher=[[Associated Press]]|via=[[CNN]]}}</ref> Its legality has been questioned by a coalition of 67 members of [[United States Congress|Congress]], led by [[Jeff Merkley]] and Debbie Wasserman Schultz.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.merkley.senate.gov/wp-content/uploads/FINAL-Alligator-Alcatraz-Oversight-Bicameral-Letter-25.08.20.pdf|title=Public letter signed by 67 members of Congress to Kristi Noem et al on August 20, 2025}}</ref>

In August 2025, U.S. district judge [[Kathleen M. Williams|Kathleen Williams]] granted a [[Injunction|preliminary injunction]] halting construction and prohibiting the government from transferring any additional detainees to the site, which was later stayed by the Court of Appeals for the 11th Circuit allowing continued operations.<ref>Luscombe, Richard. (October 2, 2025) [https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2025/oct/02/alligator-alcatraz-ron-desantis-paul-huck Husband of judge who blocked 'Alligator Alcatraz' shutdown has ties to DeSantis.] ''[[The Guardian]]''. Retrieved October 4, 2025.</ref><ref name="guardian">{{cite web|last1=Luscombe|first1=Richard|title=Alligator Alcatraz snaps back to life after judges' reprieve of Florida's migrant jail|date=7 October 2025|newspaper=[[The Guardian]]|language=en-GB|url=https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2025/oct/07/trump-alligator-alcatraz-florida|access-date=5 November 2025}}</ref>

On December 30, 2025, Trump vetoed the bipartisan Miccosukee Reserved Area Act citing the immigration detention facility. The act would have transferred 30 acres of land in the Everglades to control by the [[Miccosukee Tribe of Indians]].

State records show that $34 million in public dollars had been spent on technology and IT support by April 2026, when the Florida Division of Emergency Management said that adding phones as required by a judge, would cost $180,000 up front plus $6,000 weekly. The DEM also reported having spent millions of dollars in legal fees statewide for immigration detention over three years and hundreds of thousands of dollars on private jet flights to and from the facility and food products.<ref>Caputo, Liv. (April 27, 2026)  [https://www.wlrn.org/immigration/2026-04-27/florida-spent-34m-on-tech-it-at-everglades-lockup-but-says-phones-for-detainees-too-expensive Florida spent $34M on tech, IT at Everglades lockup, but says phones for detainees too expensive.] [[WLRN South Florida]].</ref>

In February 2026, Florida House Republicans, led by Griff Griffits of [[Panama City Beach]], introduced a successful bill, supported by Democrats, that prohibits the use of Florida emergency funding for the camp, reserving the funds only for [[natural disasters]].<ref name="auto7"/> According to Transparency Florida, a government accountability website, FDEM filed a budget amendment May 6 notifying payments of $45.3 million out of the Emergency Preparedness and Response Fund for invoices of the 2025-2026 year, before the bill passed in the Legislature. In total, FDEM has spent $458.5 million in emergency funds on immigration enforcement in the past financial year.<ref name="auto10"/>

On May 7, 2026, ''[[The New York Times]]'' reported that federal and state officials were debating whether to close the facility owing to its high operational costs. It reported that a promised reimbursement worth $608 million by the federal government for Florida to run the facility for a year had not been received by Florida officials.<ref name="Closing"/><ref>{{cite web|author=Schneider, Mike|url=https://apnews.com/article/florida-alligator-alcatraz-immigration-detention-9a43b03aab7bae27b4e080ab39cc0837|title=Appellate court pauses lawsuit over Everglades detention center due to government shutdown|publisher=[[ABC News (United States)|ABC News]]|language=en-US|url-status=live|date=October 22, 2025|access-date=November 1, 2026|archive-date=October 22, 2025|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251022223431/https://apnews.com/article/florida-alligator-alcatraz-immigration-detention-9a43b03aab7bae27b4e080ab39cc0837}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|author=Vazquez, Christina |url=https://www.local10.com/video/news/2025/10/21/is-alligator-alcatraz-a-pay-to-play-project-watchdogs-demand-transparency/|title=Is 'Alligator Alcatraz' a pay-to-play project? Watchdogs demand transparency|publisher=[[WPLG|Local 10 News]]|language=en-US|url-status=live|date=October 21, 2025|access-date=November 1, 2026|archive-date=|archive-url=}}</ref>

According to interviews published in the May 15, 2026 edition of the ''[[The San Juan Daily Star]]'', some private vendors hired by the state for the site's operations struggled to front costs, as some invoices have not been paid in over 200 days.<ref>{{cite web|author=Mazzei, Patricia; Aleaziz, Hamed|url=https://www.sanjuandailystar.com/post/florida-plans-to-close-alligator-alcatraz-vendors-are-reportedly-told|title=Florida plans to close ‘Alligator Alcatraz,' vendors are reportedly told.|newspaper=[[The San Juan Daily Star]]|language=en-US|url-status=live|date=May 15, 2026|access-date=November 1, 2026|archive-date=June 14, 2026|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260614044209/https://www.sanjuandailystar.com/post/florida-plans-to-close-alligator-alcatraz-vendors-are-reportedly-told}}</ref> In September 2026, the DeSantis administration had paid out nearly $630 million to contractors, with about $812 million in outstanding balances.<ref name="Caputo 09042026"/>

==Legal challenges==
===Native American tribal rights===
Miccosukee Tribe Chairman Talbert Cypress testified in a recent lawsuit that this is not the first time the tribe has had to [[Seminole Wars|fight for its land and rights]], affirming, "we will always stand up for our culture, our sovereignty, and for the Everglades."<ref>{{cite news|url=https://apnews.com/article/florida-alligator-alcatraz-trump-injunction-9dc2aa22f87a2a5ac8436918a8794d37|title=Florida must stop expanding 'Alligator Alcatraz' immigration center, judge says|publisher=[[Associated Press]]|first1=David |last1=Fischer|first2=Mike|last2=Schneider|first3=Freida |last3=Frisaro|date=August 21, 2025|access-date=November 1, 2026|archive-date=August 22, 2025|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250822023747/https://apnews.com/article/florida-alligator-alcatraz-trump-injunction-9dc2aa22f87a2a5ac8436918a8794d37}}</ref> There are 15 remaining traditional Miccosukee and Seminole villages, recognised as [[Indigenous people of the Everglades region]], in Big Cypress, as well as ceremonial and burial grounds and other gathering sites, Cypress testified before Congress in 2024."We live here. Our ancestors fought and died here. They are buried here," he said. "The Big Cypress is part of us, and we are a part of it."<ref>Payne, Katie. (June 26, 2025) "[https://apnews.com/article/florida-alligator-alcatraz-immigration-detention-desantis-trump-8856c0e2b9ecb8c0fb960f6e3e72a5ae Native leaders blast construction of Florida's 'Alligator Alcatraz' on land they call sacred.] [[Associated Press]]. Retrieved September 11, 2025.</ref> The [[Seminole Tribe of Florida]] was likewise in opposition citing sacred lands.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Goñi-Lessan |first=Ana |title=Seminole Tribe of Florida joins opposition to 'Alligator Alcatraz' in Everglades |url=https://www.staugustine.com/story/news/local/state/2025/07/02/seminole-tribe-calls-alligator-alcatraz-threat-to-sacred-lands-florida/84450024007/ |website=St. Augustine Record}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Environmental and Indigenous Groups Mobilize to Stop 'Alligator Alcatraz'|date=June 30, 2025|url=https://www.commondreams.org/news/environmental-groups-alligator-alcatraz |website=Common Dreams|first=Stephen |last=Prager}}</ref>

Republican Representative [[Carlos A. Giménez|Carlos Gimenez]] of Florida sponsored a bill in July 2025 which would have transferred 30 acres of land in the Everglades to control by the [[Miccosukee Tribe of Indians]] in order to avert "catastrophic flooding" and referring to the Miccosukee Tribe as "stewards of the Everglades." The Act reflected years of "bipartisan work and was intended to clarify land status and support basic protections for tribal members who have lived in this area for generations," wrote Chairman Cypress. According to Kevin Washburn, a law professor at [[University of California Berkeley]] Law, "It is rare for an administration to veto a bill for reasons wholly unrelated to the merits of the bill." Washburn added that while denying land return to a tribe is a political act, Trump's move is "highly unusual."<ref>Spotted Elk, Miacel (January 9, 2026) [https://grist.org/indigenous/the-miccosukee-tribe-blocked-alligator-alcatraz-then-trump-blocked-a-bill-to-return-their-land/ The Miccosukee Tribe blocked Alligator Alcatraz. Then Trump blocked a bill to return their land.] ''Grist''.</ref> On December 30, 2025, Trump vetoed the bipartisan Miccosukee Reserved Area Act citing the immigration detention facility.

The facility casts bright lights across sacred tribal lands where the Miccosukee people have conducted their annual [[Green Corn Ceremony]] for many generations. The intense illumination disrupts the tribe's spiritual practices and the delicate nocturnal ecosystem that depends on natural light cycles.<ref>EnviroLink. (April 30, 2026) [https://www.envirolink.org/2026/04/30/sacred-everglades-ceremonies-disrupted-as-appeals-court-allows-migrant-detention-facility-to-continue-operating/ Sacred Everglades Ceremonies Disrupted as Appeals Court Allows Migrant Detention Facility to Continue Operating.] ''EnviroLink.''</ref>

===Environmental challenge and injunction===
In June 2025, [[Betty Osceola]], a Miccosukee tribal judge and member of the Everglades Advisory Committee, organized Indigenous-led prayer gatherings and public demonstrations to highlight environmental and cultural concerns. Talbert Cypress, chairman of the [[Miccosukee]] Business Council, noted that no environmental impact research had been done and that some Native villages were within {{convert|900|ft|m}} of the camp's entrance.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Florida tribe fights new 'Alligator Alcatraz' migrant facility near Everglades homes|date=July 2, 2025|access-date=January 8, 2026|last=Louallen|first=Doc|url=https://abcnews.go.com/US/florida-tribe-fights-new-alligator-alcatraz-migrant-facility/story?id=123393299|publisher=[[ABC News (United States)|ABC News]]|language=en-US}}</ref> On June 23, 2025, [[Miami-Dade County Mayor]] [[Daniella Levine Cava]] wrote to the Florida Division and stated, "With the federal and state government investing well over $10 billion since 2019 in Everglades restoration and protection, we would appreciate a detailed analysis and report on environmental impacts of this facility to the Everglades."<ref name="AP-20250806"/>

On June 27, 2025, a coalition led by [[Friends of the Everglades]], the [[Center for Biological Diversity]], and the [[Miccosukee Tribe of Indians]], represented by [[Earthjustice]] and attorney Paul Schwiep, filed suit in a federal court seeking an injunction until a full environmental review and public-comment period are completed.<ref name="APLawsuit">{{cite news |publisher=[[Associated Press]]|date=27 June 2025 |title=Environmental groups sue to block migrant detention center rising in Florida Everglades |url=https://apnews.com/article/florida-alligator-alcatraz-history-immigration-detention-activism-796d5fae66d28de45c647241aa02d7bd |access-date=June 29, 2025}}</ref> Plaintiffs argue that the project threatens the habitat of endangered species, including that of the [[Florida panther]] and the [[Florida bonneted bat]], and violates both the [[National Environmental Policy Act]] (NEPA) and tribal cultural-resource protections.<ref>{{Cite news|last=Tabuchi |first=Hiroko|date=2025-08-08|title='Alligator Alcatraz' in the Florida Everglades Is Testing Environmental Law |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2025/08/08/climate/alligator-alcatraz-everglades-airport.htm|newspaper=[[The New York Times]]|language=en-US}}</ref>

On August 7, 2025, U.S. District Judge [[Kathleen M. Williams|Kathleen Williams]] temporarily halted construction at the facility for two weeks, while she considered if the detention center violates environmental laws. Witnesses testified that 20 acres (8 hectares) of new asphalt had been laid, while temporary tents, trailers, and other heavy equipment were at the airport.<ref>{{cite news|last1=Fischer|first1=David|title=Judge orders temporary halt to construction at Florida's 'Alligator Alcatraz' detention center |url=https://apnews.com/article/florida-detention-alligator-alcatraz-08aac166ad5fa5dfbd33a00f6be2b979 |publisher=[[Associated Press]]|language=en-US|date=August 7, 2025|access-date=November 1, 2026|archive-date=August 7, 2025|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250807195538/https://apnews.com/article/florida-detention-alligator-alcatraz-08aac166ad5fa5dfbd33a00f6be2b979}}</ref> Located in tropical wetlands, its infrastructure and sewage may be sources of both [[water pollution]] and [[light pollution]].{{fact|date=November 2026}}

Judge Williams later granted a preliminary injunction on August 21 that prohibits the government from transferring any additional detainees to the site or performing any more construction work. She also ordered the Trump administration to remove temporary fencing, industrial lighting, generators, sewage and waste receptacles from the site within 60 days.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Charalambous|first1=Peter|last2=Brown|first2= Ely|last3=Garcia |first3= Armando |title= Judge blocks transfer of new detainees to Alligator Alcatraz |url=https://abcnews.go.com/US/judge-blocks-transfer-new-detainees-alligator-alcatraz/story?id=124868357|access-date=2025-08-22|publisher=[[ABC News (United States)|ABC News]]|date=August 21, 2025|language=en-US}}</ref> Uthmeier stated that they plan to keep the ICE facility running, despite the court order.<ref>{{Cite magazine |title=Florida Outright Refuses to Shut Down "Alligator Alcatraz" |url=https://newrepublic.com/post/199563/trump-ice-immigration-florida-alligator-alcatraz|access-date=2025-08-27 |magazine=[[The New Republic]]|issn=0028-6583}}</ref>

The [[U.S. Court of Appeals for the 11th Circuit]], in a 2–1 decision early September, first stayed the injunction pending appeal, stating that because the federal government had yet to reimburse Florida's costs, federal law (the NEPA, which requires an environmental impact study) did not apply.<ref>{{Cite web|first1=Ely|last1=Brown|first2=Peter|last2=Charalambous|date=September 4, 2025|title=Appeals court allows Alligator Alcatraz to continue immigrant detention center operations |url=https://abcnews.go.com/US/appeals-court-allows-alligator-alcatraz-continue-immigrant-detention/story?id=125271773 |access-date=January 8, 2026|publisher=[[ABC News (United States)|ABC News]]|language=en-US}}</ref> The State's request for federal reimbursement had been submitted on August 7, 2025, which it did not inform the courts of.<ref>{{cite web|last=Schneider|first=Mike|date=October 14, 2025|url=https://apnews.com/article/florida-immigration-environment-alligator-alcatraz-96c118d68870b90335e3a7cffc875b9f|title=Florida officials didn't disclose funding request for 'Alligator Alcatraz' facility, lawsuit says|publisher=[[Associated Press]]|access-date=January 8, 2026}}</ref> The Appellate Court granted a second stay, citing [[2025 United States federal government shutdown|the government shutdown]].<ref>{{cite news|last=Ndonwie|first=Churchill |date=October 23, 2025|url=https://www.miamiherald.com/news/politics-government/article312610170.html |title=Appellate court pauses Alligator Alcatraz lawsuit because of government shutdown|newspaper=[[Miami Herald]]|access-date=October 24, 2025}}</ref> On August 14, Friends of the Everglades filed suit to access Florida's undisclosed records of government financing for the camp under the [[Government in the Sunshine Act]].<ref>{{cite press release|publisher=EarthJustice|date=October 14, 2025|url=https://earthjustice.org/press/2025/friends-of-the-everglades-files-suit-to-get-public-records-on-everglades-detention-center|title=Friends of the Everglades Files Suit to Get Public Records on Everglades Detention Center|access-date=January 8, 2026}}</ref> In April 2026, the US Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit ruled that the federal government could skip environmental review as the facility, considering it to be not "federally controlled", making it the first circuit court to rule on amendments Congress added to the [[National Environmental Policy Act]] in 2023.<ref>Mills, Taylor. (April 27, 2026) [https://news.bloomberglaw.com/environment-and-energy/alligator-alcatraz-ruling-opens-environmental-review-loophole 'Alligator Alcatraz' Ruling Opens Environmental Review Loophole.] [[Bloomberg Law]].</ref>

{{Infobox court case
| name = Center for Biological Diversity v. Guthrie
| court = [[Southern District of Florida]]
| judge = [[Federico A. Moreno]]
| start date = {{Start date and age|2026|5|27}}
